beats.narration: A system that survives failure still has to be affordable and fast, or it won't survive the bill. This section makes the spend visible, names the levers that move it, and then takes on the pattern that multiplies cost fastest: multi-agent orchestration.

elements.text: Cost & Orchestration

resilient isn't enough —
it has to survive the BILL
see the spend → pull the levers → tame the fan-out

beats.narration: Start by making cost visible. Three metrics on every call: token usage in and out, latency, and error rate. It's a thin wrapper logging what the API already returns. With it, a cost spike stops being a mystery on the invoice and becomes a row you can sort — and the flow that looked uniformly expensive usually turns out to have one step doing ninety percent of the spend. That step is where every optimization dollar goes. Same for latency: the slow step is rarely the one you expected.

elements.text: instrument every call: tokens · latency · errors

elements.code:
def instrumented_call(make_call, step):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    resp  = make_call()
    log_metric(step,
               resp.usage.input_tokens,
               resp.usage.output_tokens,
               latency_ms(start))
    return resp

elements.text: one step ≈ 90% of the spend — sort and see

beats.narration: The levers, once you can see. Model selection: route simple work to smaller models. Prompt and context size: every token costs, so trim what the call doesn't need. The number of tool calls: each one adds cost and latency. And streaming, which doesn't cut total time — it changes perceived time, because the first token arrives in milliseconds instead of the user staring at a spinner. One care point: when you stream with tools, a tool block isn't safe to act on until the stream closes. Act on a partial block and you hand your tools malformed input.

beats.narration: Prompt caching removes repeated work. The model processes your prompt before generating anything; normally that work is discarded and the next request recomputes it. Caching stores the work for a stable prefix — the long system prompt, the big tool schema — so later requests read it back for a tenth of the input price. Three conditions decide whether it pays. The prefix must be exactly identical, because one added word invalidates it. It must recur soon, inside the five-minute default lifetime. And it must be long enough to clear the model's minimum. Writes cost extra and reads are cheap, so the economics work when reads outnumber writes.

elements.text: prompt caching: reuse the prefix work

items.text: exactly identical — one word breaks it
long enough — clears the model's minimum

elements.text: pays when reads ≫ writes (reads ≈ 0.1×)

beats.narration: Some work doesn't need an answer now. Overnight classification, backfills, scheduled reports — the Batches API processes them asynchronously for roughly half the cost. The trade is pure: latency for money. A user is waiting? Stream it. A schedule drives it? Batch it. And batch plus cache compound: the discount cuts each request, while caching cuts the repeated prefix inside each one.

elements.text: the Batches API: latency ↔ ~half the bill

batch + cache compound:
discount × cheaper prefix

beats.narration: Now the big multiplier. The orchestrator-worker pattern: a lead agent decomposes the task, parallel subagents each work in their own context, and the lead synthesizes their results. Think of it as a hiring decision. Five researchers finish a broad survey faster than one — but you pay five salaries. Anthropic's own research system reports the numbers: a real quality gain on research that genuinely splits into independent parts, at roughly fifteen times the tokens of a normal chat, because every subagent spends its own tokens in its own context. For tightly coupled work like coding, where each step waits on the last, the multiplier buys almost nothing. One trim that helps: a capable model as the lead, cheaper models as the workers.

elements.code:
plan    = await lead.plan(task)
results = await gather(*[worker.run(s)
                         for s in plan.subtasks])
answer  = await lead.synthesize(results)

elements.text: 5 researchers = faster survey · 5 salaries
≈ 15× the tokens of a single chat
coupled work (coding): multiplier buys ~nothing
✓ capable lead · cheaper workers

beats.narration: The watch-out writes itself. A developer split a slow task across parallel subagents. Latency dropped a little, the bill tripled, and quality barely moved. The senior's diagnosis: the task didn't decompose. Each step depended on the last, so the subagents mostly waited on each other — paying the fan-out cost without the parallel benefit. Moved back to a single agent with good context, the bill fell and quality held. Orchestration isn't bad. The multiplier only buys something when the work truly runs in parallel.

beats.narration: Last rule: reliability is a floor you tune cost within, never a variable you trade down. Set the floor first — the latency ceiling, the retry budget, the pinned eval score — then optimize spend above it. Cost pressure is loud. Reliability failures are quiet, right up until they're an incident. A slightly higher bill is easier to defend than a system that doesn't work. Next: the checkpoint matches four tasks to their cost levers, then security.
